facts.title: A room that looks back
facts.body: Las Meninas (1656) places Infanta Margarita among attendants while Velázquez paints a vast canvas we cannot see. A mirror on the far wall reflects the king and queen — or the viewer standing where they stand.

facts.title: Infanta Margarita at center
facts.body: The five-year-old infanta is the bright focus of the group, yet she may be only a secondary subject next to the hidden royal sitters.

facts.title: The painter inside the picture
facts.body: Velázquez includes himself with brush and palette, claiming the dignity of painting as a liberal art at the Spanish court.

facts.title: A menina kneeling
facts.body: María Agustina Sarmiento offers the infanta a tray — court etiquette turned into gentle geometry.

facts.title: A menina curtsying
facts.body: Isabel de Velasco bends toward Margarita, framing her with ceremony.

facts.title: The mirror’s double portrait
facts.body: King Philip IV and Queen Mariana appear in the rear mirror. Whether reflection or painting-within-painting, it folds the royal gaze into the room.

facts.title: What we cannot see
facts.body: The huge canvas’s face is turned away. The painting withholds its own subject — a riddle at the heart of the masterpiece.

facts.title: Silhouette in the doorway
facts.body: José Nieto, the queen’s aposentador, pauses on the back stairs, catching light like a second author of the scene.

facts.title: A sleeping mastiff
facts.body: A large dog rests in the foreground, unimpressed by empire — Velázquez’s dry humor.

facts.title: Maribarbola and Nicolasito
facts.body: Court dwarfs stand at right, part of the Habsburg household’s everyday theatre and another measure of the room’s social scale.
